note.en: Indra for the Devas and Virochana for the Asuras come as fellow pupils to Prajapati and study together for thirty-two years.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Seventh Khanda - 'Indra went from the Devas, Virokana from the Asuras, and both, without having communicated with each other, approached Pragapati, holding fuel in their hands, as is the custom for pupils approaching their master'

verification.notes: Chandogya VIII, 7, 2-3 has Indra and Virochana approach Prajapati together as fellow pupils and dwell there thirty-two years.

note.en: Virochana takes the body to be the Self and teaches that doctrine to the Asuras, which the Upanishad marks as the doctrine that perishes.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Eighth Khanda - 'Virokana, satisfied in his heart, went to the Asuras and preached that doctrine to them, that the self (the body) alone is to be worshipped'

verification.notes: Chandogya VIII, 8, 4 has Virochana carry away the mistaken teaching that the body is the Self and preach it to the Asuras.

note.en: Unlike Virochana, Indra sees that a self identified with the body perishes with it, and returns for further teaching on the true Self.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Ninth Khanda - 'Taking fuel in his hand he came again as a pupil to Pragapati' after seeing that the bodily self 'will perish in fact as soon as the body perishes'

verification.notes: Chandogya VIII, 9, 1-3 has Indra alone detect the flaw in the bodily self and return as a pupil for further instruction on the Self.

note.en: The instruction Indra pursues through successive stays with Prajapati is the identification of the Self with Brahman.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Seventh Khanda - Pragapati: 'The person that is seen in the eye, that is the Self. This is what I have said. This is the immortal, the fearless, this is Brahman'

verification.notes: Chandogya VIII, 7, 4 records the teaching identifying the Self with Brahman that Indra receives from Prajapati.

note.en: Indra is the central pupil of the Chandogya's longest instruction sequence, returning repeatedly until the true Self is taught.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Seventh to Ninth Khandas - Prajapati tells Indra 'Live with me another thirty-two years'

verification.notes: Indra appears across Chandogya VIII, 7-9 as the persistent pupil in the Prajapati instruction cycle.

note.en: Virochana's only Upanishadic role is as the Asura pupil who departs satisfied with an incomplete answer.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Eighth Prapathaka, Seventh and Eighth Khandas - 'Virokana from the Asuras' approaches Pragapati and departs 'satisfied in his heart'

verification.notes: Virochana appears in Chandogya VIII, 7-8 as Indra's Asura counterpart in the Prajapati episode.

note.en: Narada approaches Sanatkumara as a pupil, and the whole seventh Prapathaka of the Chandogya is the instruction that follows.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Seventh Prapathaka, First Khanda - 'Narada approached Sanatkumara and said, Teach me, Sir!'

verification.notes: Chandogya VII, 1, 1 opens with Narada formally approaching Sanatkumara for instruction, and VII, 26, 2 closes with Sanatkumara showing him the other side of darkness.

note.en: The closing sentence of the Chandogya's seventh Prapathaka names the teaching as completed from Sanatkumara to Narada.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Seventh Prapathaka, Twenty-sixth Khanda - 'The venerable Sanatkumara showed to Narada, after his faults had been rubbed out, the other side of darkness'

verification.notes: Chandogya VII, 26, 2 states the completed transmission from Sanatkumara to Narada.

note.en: Narada's request is framed as the insufficiency of textual learning without knowledge of the Self.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Seventh Prapathaka, First Khanda - Narada: 'But, Sir, with all this I know the Mantras only, the sacred books, I do not know the Self'

verification.notes: Chandogya VII, 1, 3 has Narada confess that his mastery of the Vedas has not given him knowledge of the Self.

note.en: Narada is the questioner whose successive requests for something better drive the whole of Chandogya VII.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Seventh Prapathaka, First to Twenty-sixth Khandas - Narada as the questioner throughout, asking 'Sir, is there something better than a name?'

verification.notes: Narada is the named interlocutor of the entire seventh Prapathaka of the Chandogya Upanishad.

note.en: Sanatkumara is the teacher of Chandogya VII, whom the text's closing line identifies with Skanda.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Seventh Prapathaka, Twenty-sixth Khanda - 'They call Sanatkumara Skanda, yea, Skanda they call him'

verification.notes: Sanatkumara is the teacher of the whole seventh Prapathaka of the Chandogya and is identified there with Skanda.

note.en: Uddalaka Aruni is the father-teacher of the Chandogya's sixth Prapathaka.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Sixth Prapathaka, First Khanda - 'To him his father (Uddalaka, the son of Aruna) said: Svetaketu, go to school'

verification.notes: Aruni, that is Uddalaka Aruni, is the teaching father of Chandogya VI and appears again in the Kaushitaki and Brihadaranyaka.

note.en: Aruni's opening question to his son sets out the knowledge of the one by which all else is known.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Sixth Prapathaka, First Khanda - 'have you ever asked for that instruction by which we hear what cannot be heard, by which we perceive what cannot be perceived, by which we know what cannot be known?'

verification.notes: Chandogya VI, 1, 3 has Uddalaka Aruni pose the question that opens his teaching on the one reality by which all is known.

note.en: Aruni teaches the Self through sleep, hunger and thirst as successive demonstrations of the one True.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Chandogya Upanishad, Sixth Prapathaka, Eighth Khanda - 'Uddalaka Aruni said to his son Svetaketu: Learn from me the true nature of sleep (svapna). When a man sleeps here, then, my dear son, he becomes united with the True'

verification.notes: Chandogya VI, 8, 1 has Uddalaka Aruni teach that in sleep a man goes to his own Self.

note.en: The Kaushitaki opens with Aruni deputing his son to a sacrifice, then taking fuel in hand and coming to Chitra Gangyayani as a pupil himself.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Kaushitaki Upanishad, First Adhyaya - 'Kitra Gangyayani, forsooth, wishing to perform a sacrifice, chose Aruni (Uddalaka, to be his chief priest). But Aruni sent his son, Svetaketu'

verification.notes: Kaushitaki I, 1 opens with Aruni chosen as chief priest, sending his son in his place, and then himself coming to Chitra as a pupil with fuel in hand.

note.en: Yama's first boon names Nachiketa's father as Auddalaki Aruni; at Katha I, 1, 1 the same father is called Vajasravasa.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - Yama: 'Through my favour Auddalaki Aruni, thy father, will know thee, and be again towards thee as he was before'

verification.notes: Katha I, 1, 11 names Nachiketa's father as Auddalaki Aruni in Yama's granting of the first boon.

note.en: Nachiketa's first boon is his father's goodwill; Yama identifies the father as Auddalaki Aruni.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - Nachiketa: 'I choose that Gautama, my father, be pacified, kind, and free from anger towards me'; Yama names him 'Auddalaki Aruni, thy father'

verification.notes: Katha I, 1, 10-11 has Nachiketa ask for his father's goodwill and Yama name that father Auddalaki Aruni.

note.en: Yama grants Nachiketa three boons after his three-night wait, and the third boon is the teaching on what survives death.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - Yama: 'O Brahmana, as thou, a venerable guest, hast dwelt in my house three nights without eating, therefore choose now three boons'

verification.notes: Katha I, 1, 9 begins the instruction in which Yama grants Nachiketa three boons and teaches him what follows death.

note.en: Nachiketa is the pupil of Death himself, refusing wealth and long life in favour of the question of the Self.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - Nachiketa asks his boons of Death, saying 'What will be the work of Yama... which to-day he has to do unto me?'

verification.notes: Katha I, 1, 5-11 has Nachiketa enter Yama's abode and receive instruction from him as his pupil.

note.en: Nachiketa is the boy whose faith and refusal of lesser boons frames the entire Katha Upanishad.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - 'faith entered into the heart of Nakiketas, who was still a boy'

verification.notes: Nachiketa is the named pupil of the whole Katha Upanishad, introduced at Katha I, 1, 2.

note.en: Nachiketa's questioning of Death moves from the heavenly world to the Self that death does not touch.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Katha Upanishad, First Adhyaya, First Valli - 'In the heaven-world there is no fear; thou art not there, O Death, and no one is afraid on account of old age'

verification.notes: Katha I, 1, 12 has Nachiketa press Yama past the fire-sacrifice toward what remains when the body dies.

note.en: Indra makes his own self-knowledge the boon he grants Pratardana, and teaches him prana as the conscious self.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Kaushitaki Upanishad, Third Adhyaya - Indra: 'Know me only; that is what I deem most beneficial for man, that he should know me'; and 'I am prana, meditate on me as the conscious self'

verification.notes: Kaushitaki III, 1-2 has Indra instruct Pratardana son of Divodasa on prana as the conscious self.

note.en: Pratardana asks Indra to choose the boon for him, and receives instruction rather than a gift.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Kaushitaki Upanishad, Third Adhyaya - 'Pratardana, forsooth, the son of Divodasa (king of Kasi), came by means of fighting and strength to the beloved abode of Indra'

verification.notes: Kaushitaki III, 1 has Pratardana reach Indra's abode and receive instruction in place of an ordinary boon.

note.en: Pratardana is the royal interlocutor of the Kaushitaki's third Adhyaya on prana.

sources.source_chapter_or_section: Kaushitaki Upanishad, Third Adhyaya - Pratardana as Indra's interlocutor, objecting that 'the pranas become one'

verification.notes: Pratardana is the named questioner of the third Adhyaya of the Kaushitaki Upanishad.
